Re-rendered PDF page 72 bottom-right and PDF page 73 top-left from the on-disk file and viewed them, plus the compiler full-page renders / : the heading '9.1.4 Word stress' sits at the foot of the right column of printed p. 57 (page number 57 visible below it) and the single sentence 'Ndao word stress is penultimate.' sits at the head of the left column of printed p. 58, immediately before '9.2 Noun phrase constituents, verbs, clause modifiers'. Quote is verbatim (heading + one sentence). The scanned files scanned/ and scanned/ agree. Surrounding section read: 9.0 Introduction says Ndao is the language of Ndao…
new_statements.relation_note: Catalog penultimate stress is penultimate stress on all word lengths; Walker's one-sentence statement 'Ndao word stress is penultimate' is the same placement. Walker gives no domain, weight, secondary-stress or exception detail for Ndao, so it does not refine the catalog beyond confirming it. Note the language is called 'Ndao' throughout; Walker treats it as closely related to but distinct from Sawu (the informants were from Ndao island, interviewed in Kupang 1975-76).
new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress in Ndao (Dhao) falls on the penultimate syllable; the section consists of this single sentence, with no examples, exceptions or mention of secondary stress for Ndao.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Nothing stated for Ndao. For Sawu (not Ndao) the same work says in 2.6 (p. 7): 'Words of four-or-more syllables are stressed on every second syllable from the end. e.g wo'peka'lae "ankle"', and analyses stressed long vowels as disyllabic 'CVV with predictable penultimate stress; Walker does not say whether these details carry over to Ndao.
new_statements.exceptions: None for Ndao. Section 9.1.2 notes that apart from 'a few words which have four or more syllables' an Ndao root has the same (C1V1)(C2)V2(C3)V3 structure as Sawu; nothing is said about stress in those longer words. The only other 'penultimate' hit in ch. 9 (p. 63) is a historical note about a penultimate high vowel conditioning *-a > -e, not about stress.
new_statements.identity_note: Walker 1982 describes the language of Ndao and Nuse islands under the name 'Ndao' (= Dhao, dhao1237), based on two speakers recorded in Kupang in 1975-76; he treats it as a separate language from Sawu (Hawu) despite Jonker's and Fox's earlier 'dialect of Savunese' view. The much longer Sawu stress discussion in the same volume (2.6, pp. 7-8) concerns Sawu (sabu1255), not Dhao.

audit.reasoning: The record codes Dhao as fixed penultimate on the strength of a Wikipedia sentence, with empty quote/cite/loc/grade fields and no copies we hold, so the verbatim check is impossible (verification pending (no copy obtained)). Glottolog's top descriptive reference, Balukh 2020 (397-pp Leiden/LOT reference grammar), is open access; I downloaded it (423-page PDF with text) and read §2.3.3 'Stress Assignment' (pp. 62-64) and the related syllable sections. It states unambiguously that Dhao has fixed, non-contrastive penultimate stress, retained under prefixation and reduplication, with secondary stress on the initial syllable of four-syllable words, long vowels counted as two syllables so stress is on the penultimate vowel, and the same rule over compounds. Walker 1982 (NUSA 13, image-only; scanned of two pages at 200 dpi, one tesseract at a time) independently says 'Ndao word stress is penultimate' (§9.1.4, pp. 57-58). Bo

sources.citation: Balukh, Jermy Immanuel. 2020. A Grammar of Dhao: An Endangered Austronesian Language in Eastern Indonesia. PhD dissertation, Leiden University. LOT Dissertation Series 570. Amsterdam: LOT. xxvi+397 pp.
sources.quote: p.62: "Dhao has fixed stress, which is on penultimate syllables. Stress placement does not distinguish meaning, therefore, it is not necessary to mark stress in the orthography. As mentioned previously, stress is predictable on the penultimate syllable (see Walker, 1982; Grimes, 2010)." p.63: "The analysis above confirms that Dhao has fixed stress. Stress is not contrastive. Disyllabic roots have stress on the first syllable which is retained when roots take prefixes ... For trisyllabic roots, the main stress falls on the penultimate syllable and is retained when prefixed with pa-, as in [maˈm
sources.locator: §2.3.3 'Stress Assignment', printed pp. 62-64 (pp. 88-90); also §2.1 p. 27 (PDF 53), §2.3.1 pp. 55-61, §2.2.3.8 p. 53, ch. 5 p. 179 (PDF 205), Summary p. 386 (PDF 412)
sources.note: The only reference grammar of Dhao, with a dedicated stress section (§2.3.3, pp. 62-64); our record cites Wikipedia's paraphrase of it with no grade or locator.
